content.text: The text examines architectural ornament: chamfers, beads, dogtooth, dentils, rolls, bases, shafts, capitals, cornices, archivolts, roofs, and wall decoration. It praises ornament that grows from construction, expresses strength, naturalism, labor, and human intention, while condemning rustication, Renaissance formalism, excessive finials, and machine-made decoration. Gothic architecture is contrasted favorably with classical and Renaissance work, especially in Venice, Verona, Lucca, Pavia, and northern France. The author distinguishes concave and convex capital families as discipline and freedom. He argues art should explain nature rather than “correct” it. He travels from Padua along the Brenta to Dolo and Mestre, then enters a gondola and travels across the lagoon toward Venice, whose history and architecture he describes.
